clue.text: Balls being inverted, used glue — overwhelming amount

indicators.note: being inverted means turned upside down, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Ed Balls is a former Labour cabinet minister, now a TV presenter

indicators.note: used here means worked over and reshaped, so the letters of glue take a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone's balls have been flipped over, with a vast amount of glue used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is not testicles but Ed Balls, the former Labour minister: ED 'being inverted' gives DE, and 'used' rearranges GLUE into LUGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deluge is a great flood, so figuratively it is an overwhelming quantity of anything.

clue.text: Tension relaxer produced by CID employee cut by criminal teen

indicators.note: by here means beside, so the two pieces are set next to each other
cut means shortened, so the word for the CID employee loses its tail

parts.note: a detective works for the CID, the Criminal Investigation Department of a British police force

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters of teen are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A detective has tensions eased by a young offender's arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: DETECTIVE is 'cut' to DET, its usual abbreviation, and 'by' sets it beside ENTE, which 'criminal' makes from TEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Détente is an easing of hostility between states, a slackening of political strain.

clue.text: 'Light unit' initially unveiled at Rio and America: suitable for the Sunaks' lifestyle?

parts.note: the lux is the SI unit of illumination

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of unveiled is used

explanation.surface: A product launch unveiled in Rio and America, pitched at the very rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Light unit' look like a product name, but it is a physics unit. Rishi Sunak, the former Prime Minister, and his wife Akshata Murty are famously wealthy, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Sunaks' wealthy way of life is a case of the sumptuous comfort the answer describes.

clue.text: Gum extremely flabby with teeth protruding

indicators.note: extremely is read as 'at the extremes', so only the two end letters of flabby are taken

explanation.surface: An unflattering dental description: slack gums and buck teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gum' sits next to teeth, so it looks like part of the mouth, but it is the sticky substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal sense: goofy teeth are buck teeth, ones that stick out.

clue.text: Piss taken at the doctor's?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading is mockery, since taking the piss is British slang for making fun of someone; the setter means urine literally collected
the place where a urine sample is handed over for testing

explanation.surface: Sounds like someone being mocked at the GP's surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: the question mark flags that 'piss taken' should be read literally rather than as the slang for mockery.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic definition: a urine sample collected by a doctor for testing is known as a specimen.

clue.text: State staff finally ready to take the piss

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of ready is used

explanation.surface: The employees of some state are finally poised to mock someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but it is a stick. Take the piss is British slang for to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang equivalent: to parody someone is to mock them by imitation, which in British slang is taking the piss.

clue.text: Adversary makes political party sore

explanation.surface: An opponent leaves a political party smarting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sore' reads as annoyed, which suits a party upset by a rival, but it means physically tender.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a rival competing against you in a contest is your adversary.

clue.text: Muck — there's a lot surrounding Labour leader

indicators.note: surrounding means lying all around something, so the word for 'a lot' is placed on both sides of the leader's letter

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Labour leader is surrounded by plenty of dirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' looks like the party's head, but it is only the first letter of Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: mulch is rotting organic matter spread over soil, the sort of stuff a gardener would call muck.

clue.text: Negative Poles peak without a break

parts.note: N and S, the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Gloomy Polish climbers head for the summit without resting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; in crosswords it usually gives the two poles, N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: continuing with no pause or interruption.

clue.text: Biden's son in the view of some Republicans: "Corrupt detox grad!"

definitions.text: Biden's son in the view of some Republicans

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or twisted from its proper form, so the letters of the phrase are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A Republican jeer at Hunter Biden as a crooked graduate of rehab.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunter Biden, son of President Joe Biden, went through addiction treatment and was charged over unpaid taxes, so both the fodder and the answer belong to the Republican attack on him.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: Republicans accused Hunter Biden of evading his taxes, so this is what they called him.

clue.text: Try sand to shift balls

parts.note: a go is a try, an attempt

indicators.note: to shift is to move about, so the letters of sand are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An attempt to move sand that turns into balls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to shift' turns SAND into NADS, after GO for a try.
explanation.definitionFit: Gonads are the sex glands, and testicles are slangily called balls.

clue.text: Material only about Biden's end

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fabric used in stockings, ropes and clothing, so it is a material.

clue.text: Deny bust covers bottom of jumper, like a geek

indicators.note: covers means wraps round, so the rearranged letters go either side of the single one
bust means broken, so the letters of deny are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: bottom of a word in an across clue is its last letter

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken; a jumper is a British word for a sweater

explanation.surface: A denial that a bust is covered by the bottom of a sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' rearranges DENY as NEDY, which 'covers' R, the 'bottom of' jumper, after NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerdy means socially awkward and obsessively studious, which is how one describes a geek.

clue.text: It's grand to break into naked jog

indicators.note: a burglar who breaks into a house ends up inside it

explanation.surface: Someone declares that it would be great to set off on a naked run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' reads as 'great', and 'jog' as running, which suit a streaker; they are G for a thousand pounds and a gentle push.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to jog someone's elbow is to give it a small push.

clue.text: (& 24ac.) Latest advice bound to restrict Times and Independent

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the word for bound holds the newspaper letters inside it

parts.note: T = time, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A tip-off that new rules are set to muzzle two national newspapers, The Times and The Independent.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make Times and Independent look like the newspapers; they are just the abbreviations T and I. The answer runs on into 24 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a hot tip is a piece of fresh, inside information, the newest guidance on offer.

clue.text: Early Viking leaders loved balls getting developed

indicators.note: leaders means the first letters of the two words

parts.note: the words whose first letters are taken

indicators.note: to balls up something is to make a mess of it, so the letters of loved are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'leaders' takes EV from Early Viking, and 'balls', as in balls-up, rearranges LOVED as OLVED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evolved has grown and changed by gradual stages, so it has developed.

clue.text: You've tangled with Mrs I. looking for sexual arousal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangled with' reads as having an affair with Mrs I., which suits the sexual theme, but it scrambles the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive definition: voyeurism is gaining sexual pleasure from watching others, looking in order to be aroused.

clue.text: Lose erection (dead poor circulation)

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'circulation' looks like the medical cause, but it rearranges POOR into ROOP, after D for dead.

clue.text: Outlaw's corset is tight with article concealed

something concealed is hidden inside, so the article is tucked in among the other letters

explanation.surface: A bandit's corset is laced tight, with some item smuggled inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' reads as a description of the laced corset, but it means drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb synonym: to outlaw someone is to cast them out of society, to exclude them.

clue.text: Who won't stand for a drunken spree?

definitions.meaning: someone who bends rather than standing up straight
British slang for a long session of heavy drinking

explanation.surface: Asks who would refuse to put up with a drinking binge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Won't stand for' reads as won't tolerate, but 'for' is only a link: the first sense is literally one who bends instead of standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: one who bends is literally a bender, and in British slang the word also means a drinking binge.

clue.text: Hard up lead broadcaster sounding croaky

indicators.note: lead means the first letter, the one leading the word

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken
Sky is a British satellite television broadcaster

explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' takes U from up, between H for hard and SKY, the British satellite broadcaster.

clue.text: Snag on being married: wife leaves — to get married

to get here means the wordplay before it combines to produce the answer that the last word defines

indicators.note: leaves means goes away from, so the letter for wife is taken out

parts.note: to be married is to be wed

explanation.walkthrough: 'wife leaves' takes the W out of WED, leaving ED; HITCH sits 'on' it, above it in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting hitched is an informal idiom for marrying, so a hitched couple are wedded.

clue.text: Shifting Carter involved one's being on the inside

clue.text: Name implicated in sneaky reform

clue.text: Very dull duke (English) put in list

clue.text: Stupendous housing tip

clue.text: Hospital needs a number one — and capital

clue.text: "One has to follow Blunt's command"

clue.text: For the record, desist from wrapping rod round Mordaunt's head!

clue.text: Act like a witness going topless — most gross!

explanation.surface: A witness strips to the waist, to universal disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests a Page Three scene, but it just drops the first letter. 'Gross' reads as disgusting, but here it means fat.
